## Overview

The Vikings were a seafaring people originally from Scandinavia, including present-day Norway, Denmark, and Sweden. From the late 8th to the late 11th centuries, they raided, pirated, traded, and settled across parts of Europe, voyaging as far as the Mediterranean, North Africa, the Middle East, Greenland, and Vinland. Their settlements and governments extended through the British Isles, the Faroe Islands, Iceland, Greenland, Normandy, and the Baltic coast, as well as along the Dnieper and Volga trade routes. They spoke Old Norse and used runes. Most Vikings were farmers, fishermen, craftsmen, and traders. Their importance in folk culture lies in their language, runestones, ships, settlements, craft production, religious practices, laws, art, and architecture.

## Material culture

### Clothing & dress

 They state only that popular representations commonly show Vikings wearing horned helmets, while there is no evidence that they wore them; the horned helmet became a costume element in the 19th century.

### Architecture

Viking architecture included settlements and governments established in the British Isles, the Faroe Islands, Iceland, Greenland, Normandy, and along the Baltic coast and Eastern European trade routes. The archaeological record provides knowledge of rural and urban settlement. The Vikings constructed the defence fortification of Danevirke in and around Hedeby, which remained in use throughout the Viking Age and until 1864. Jomsborg was described as a semi-legendary Viking stronghold on the southern coast of the Baltic Sea, existing between the 960s and 1043, although its exact location and existence have not been established.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

 Archaeology is described as providing evidence about crafts and production, ships, military equipment, trading networks, and pagan and Christian religious artefacts and practices. The Vikings traded goods including furs, tusks, seal fat used for boat sealant, and slaves along the Volga.

### Jewelry & body adornment

 They mention pagan and Christian religious artefacts in the archaeological record.

## Music & performance

 They state that the Vikings produced no literary legacy as a generally non-literate culture, although they used an alphabet and made inscriptions in runes. The sources also mention skaldic poetry attributed to court poets of the 10th and 11th centuries. Icelandic vernacular literature developed in the 12th through 14th centuries, and traditions connected with the Viking Age were written down in the Icelandic sagas.

## Dance & theatre

 They mention sagas, skaldic poetry, and literary writings connected with the Viking Age.

## Festivals & rituals

 They state that the Vikings initially followed the Old Norse religion and became Christians over the 8th–12th centuries. Religious change was connected with the establishment of dioceses in Denmark and Norway during the 11th century and with the organisation of Christianity in Sweden. By 1103, the first archbishopric in Scandinavia was founded at Lund, Scania, then part of Denmark.

The sources describe Christianity as transforming older ideologies and lifestyles. The assimilation of the Scandinavian kingdoms into European Christendom altered the aspirations of rulers and overseas travellers and changed relations with neighbouring peoples.

## Foodways

 They state that the Norse regularly travelled along the Volga with trade goods including furs, tusks, seal fat for boat sealant, and slaves. The sources also identify farming, fishing, craftsmanship, and trade among the occupations of most Vikings.

## Oral tradition & literature

The Vikings spoke Old Norse and made short, formulaic inscriptions in runes. Most contemporary written sources about them were produced by Christian and Islamic communities outside Scandinavia, often by authors affected by Viking activity. After the consolidation of the church and the assimilation of Scandinavia and its colonies into medieval Christian culture, native written sources appeared in Latin and Old Norse.

In Iceland, vernacular literature developed in the 12th through 14th centuries. Traditions connected with the Viking Age were written down in Icelandic sagas and chronicles. A literal interpretation of these medieval prose narratives is considered doubtful, but the sources identify skaldic poetry attributed to court poets of the 10th and 11th centuries, exposed family trees, self-images, and ethical values as significant materials. Old Norse place names and words also preserve evidence of Viking language, culture, settlement, and activities. Examples named in the source include Egilsay, Ormskirk, Meols, Snaefell, Ravenscar, Vinland, Kaupanger, Tórshavn, Odense, York, Swansea, and Tocqueville.

## Language & religion

The Vikings spoke Old Norse, a language whose influence remains visible in Swedish, Norwegian, Danish, Faroese, and Icelandic. They wrote inscriptions in runes. Writing in Latin letters was introduced to Scandinavia with Christianity, and native documentary sources before the late 11th and early 12th centuries were limited. In the Northern Isles of Shetland and Orkney, Old Norse replaced the local languages and later developed into the extinct Norn language.

For most of the Viking Age, the Vikings followed the Old Norse religion. They became Christians over the 8th–12th centuries, while Christianity took root in Denmark and Norway through the establishment of dioceses in the 11th century and began to organise itself more effectively in Sweden. The sources describe a gradual transformation of older ideologies and lifestyles rather than a single uniform religious transition.
